paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Norman Rockwell is often called ‘America’s Painter’. His career overlapped with the key art movements of the 20th century, but while other artists were experimenting with abstraction, Rockwell was heading in the opposite direction. His paintings were about storytelling, about everyday people and things: snoozing dogs, schoolchildren and family station wagons. America was a nation of immigrants who lacked universally shared traditions; it had to invent some. So it came up with Thanksgiving, baseball and Norman Rockwell.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Rockwell was born in New York City in 1894, the son of a textile salesman. He attributed his interest in art to his slight physique growing up. As a child, he felt overshadowed by his older brother, Jarvis, a first-rate athlete. Norman, by contrast, was thin and awkward, and squinted at the world through large glasses. But his art skills became apparent at a young age. Rockwell hadn’t even turned 16 when he received his first paid commission: a set of four Christmas cards requested by a neighbor.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Rockwell wanted mainly one thing, to work for the Saturday Evening Post, the most widely read magazine in the country with a circulation of over 4 million. Having proven his talent as an artist for other smaller magazines, he was given a chance in 1916. Rockwell’s first cover for the Post, called ‘Baby Carriage,’ remains one of his most psychologically intense works. A boy who appears to be about 13, dressed formally in a suit and tie, is taking his baby sister out for some fresh air. He is pushing her in a stroller when he runs into two friends, dressed in baseball uniforms and heading off to a game. They tease and laugh at the humiliated boy as he hurries along, trying to escape their ridicule. The cover was wildly popular, and Rockwell became an instant success.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: During the Second World War, Rockwell was inspired upon hearing a speech by President Franklin Roosevelt. Drawing on themes from what he’d heard, Rockwell created four paintings, titled ‘The Four Freedoms’, as posters for the US government’s Office of War Information. Perhaps the most beloved of these, ‘Freedom from Want’, depicts a family dinner on Thanksgiving Day – an annual, traditional north American holiday. The children are gathered happily around the dinner table. No one is even noticing the massive roasted turkey or the gray-haired grandmother solemnly placing it in front of them. In contrast to older, more traditional depictions of Thanksgiving dinner, which show the pre-meal as a moment of grace – heads lowered, praying hands raised to lips – Rockwell paints a table at which no one is giving thanks. This, then, is the subject of this painting: not just the sanctity of American customs, but the casual reaction with which Americans treat them.

Perhaps the most beloved of these, ‘Freedom from Want’, depicts a family dinner on Thanksgiving Day – an annual, traditional north American holiday. The children are gathered happily around the dinner table. No one is even noticing the massive roasted turkey or the gray-haired grandmother solemnly placing it in front of them. In contrast to older, more traditional depictions of Thanksgiving dinner, which show the pre-meal as a moment of grace – heads lowered, praying hands raised to lips – Rockwell paints a table at which no one is giving thanks. This, then, is the subject of this painting: not just the sanctity of American customs, but the casual reaction with which Americans treat them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Another painting, ‘Before the Shot’, takes us into a doctor’s office as a boy stands on a wooden chair awaiting an injection from the doctor. He is carefully reading the framed medical diploma hanging on the wall. He wants to reassure himself that the doctor is sufficiently qualified to perform this procedure. Rockwell had hired a young child from his small town to be his model, and one night Rockwell surprised the boy’s family by stopping by their house unannounced. He was carrying the painting and apparently needed to make sure he had correctly represented the exact color of the boy’s grayish-green pants. It’s an anecdote that reminds us of his extraordinary focus on the smallest details.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For two 1960 covers of the Saturday Evening Post magazine, Rockwell was asked to paint portraits of both the presidential candidates that year. Richard Nixon and Jack Kennedy. Rockwell did not care for Nixon, and he very much admired Kennedy. Yet in his studio, as he worked on the two portraits side by side, he put his politics aside and suppressed any sign of favoritism. He carefully made certain that neither subject’s face flashed more of a smile than the other.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Journalists who interviewed Rockwell at his studio were charmed by his boyish appearance and great modesty. He would respond to compliments by knocking on wood as a sign of luck and claiming that his career was about to collapse. Asked about his artistic gifts, he insisted he was merely an illustrator and not an artist. Perhaps he was being defensive; he couldn’t be rejected by the art world if he rejected it first. Yet Rockwell held no resentment against the abstract painters of the time. In fact, he rather admired them, even complimenting them in a magazine: ‘If I were young, I would paint that way myself.’

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: After working for five decades at the Saturday Evening Post, Rockwell left in 1963, but he continued to illustrate for various publications, in particular Look magazine. He became more absorbed in painting social issues and current events like civil rights, poverty and space exploration. In 1977, he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the United States of America’s highest civilian honor, for his ‘vivid and affectionate portraits of our country’. In all, Rockwell painted more than 4,000 works of art, and today many of them still hang in some of the most prestigious museums in the US, and even in the United Nations Building in New York.
